question.problem:
Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨x,\,z,\,y⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined in Cartesian coordinates as $z=\frac{1}{2}x-y-1$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 3.$ Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S$ with respect to the upward-pointing unit normal vector $n.$

*Hint: You're given that the fundamental vector product of $S$ with respect to its canonical parametrization is $||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}||=\frac{3}{2}.$*
question.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that our surface $z=\frac{1}{2}x-y-1$ can be written using the dot product as 

$$
⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨-\frac{1}{2},\,1,\,1⟩}_{⏟}}_{\overset{~}{n}}=-1,\,\text{or}\,⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨\frac{1}{2},\,-1,\,-1⟩}_{⏟}}_{-\overset{~}{n}}=1.
$$

Since we require an upward-pointing normal vector to our surface $S,$ we must select one where the $z$-component is positive. This gives us the normal vector

$$
\overset{~}{n}=⟨-\frac{1}{2},\,1,\,1⟩.
$$

Normalizing this vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨-\frac{1}{2},\,1,\,1⟩}{\sqrt{{(-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}⟨-\frac{1}{2},\,1,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨-1,\,2,\,2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $z=\frac{1}{2}x-y-1$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨x,\,z,\,y⟩\cdot \frac{1}{3}⟨-1,\,2,\,2⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨x,\,\frac{1}{2}x-y-1,\,y⟩\cdot ⟨-1,\,2,\,2⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(-x+(x-2y-2)+2y) \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}(-\frac{2}{3})\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-\frac{2}{3})\cdot ||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}||\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-\frac{2}{3})\cdot \frac{3}{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-\frac{\cancel{2}}{\cancel{3}})\cdot \frac{\cancel{3}}{\cancel{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-1\,\text{d}A \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{3}\,\text{d}y\cdot {\int }_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-3\cdot 1 \\  & =-3\end{aligned}
$$
